entries.name: Kievan Rus'
entries.region: Eastern Europe, from the Baltic to the Black Sea (Dnieper, Volkhov, Upper Volga)
entries.settlement: river-port towns on the Dnieper and Volkhov, a prince's court and a veche (assembly) in each
monuments: golden gates of Kyiv and Vladimir
trade: furs and wax to Byzantium and the Islamic world
entries.beliefs: East Slavic paganism to 988, then Orthodox Christianity
entries.fell_by: fragmentation into rival principalities; Mongol conquest 1237-1240
entries.notes: The crucible of the East Slavic peoples; Russians, Ukrainians and Belarusians all claim its legacy.

entries.name: Muscovites (Tsardom of Russia)
entries.region: Northeastern Russia, expanding outward from Moscow
entries.settlement: walled Kremlin-citadel towns; a boyar service nobility bound to the tsar; autocracy
trade: English and Dutch goods via Archangel
entries.beliefs: Orthodox Christianity; Moscow as the Third Rome
entries.fell_by: never fell: transformed into the Russian Empire by Peter I in 1721
entries.notes: Grew from a Mongol tax-collecting appanage into a Eurasian empire; the yam post and census underpinned it.

entries.name: Novgorod Republic
entries.region: Northwestern Russia (Novgorod and Pskov)
entries.settlement: a merchant republic run by a veche; boyars elected posadniks; close ties to the Baltic trade
trade: furs, wax, honey and hides via the Hanseatic League
entries.beliefs: Orthodox Christianity
entries.fell_by: absorbed by Muscovy; Ivan III carried the veche bell to Moscow in 1478
entries.notes: Medieval Europe's most northerly trading republic; birch-bark letters show widespread literacy.

entries.name: Poles (Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth)
entries.region: Poland (Vistula and Oder basins); Commonwealth lands to the Dnieper
entries.settlement: open-field villages under szlachta (noble) estates; royal and chartered free towns; a sjem parliament
trade: grain down the Vistula to Gdansk
timber, tar and potash to the Baltic
entries.beliefs: Roman Catholicism, holding against Orthodox and Protestant neighbors
entries.fell_by: partitioned by Russia, Prussia and Austria, 1772-1795; restored as a state in 1918
entries.notes: The Commonwealth elected its kings and guaranteed noble liberties; the liberum veto froze its politics.

entries.name: Lithuanians (Grand Duchy)
entries.region: Lithuania and Ruthenian lands (modern Belarus and Ukraine)
entries.settlement: pagan hill-fort cores, later castle towns; from 1569 in union with Poland (Union of Lublin)
trade: amber, furs, timber and grain through Baltic ports
entries.beliefs: Baltic paganism (last in Europe, to 1387), then Catholicism
entries.fell_by: absorbed into the Russian Empire in the partitions of 1795
entries.notes: At its height the largest state in Europe: pagan rulers of Orthodox Ruthenian subjects.

entries.name: Hungarians (Magyars)
entries.region: Pannonian Basin (Hungary, Transylvania, Vojvodina)
entries.settlement: villages under county nobles; fortified border castles; Budapest as twin capital
entries.beliefs: steppe shamanism at arrival (895), then Catholicism (St Stephen, 1000)
entries.fell_by: central Hungary under Ottoman rule 1541-1686; Habsburg crown thereafter; Trianon 1920 cut its lands
entries.notes: Steppe horsemen who settled the Pannonian plain; a Finno-Ugric language amid Slavic and German neighbors.

entries.name: Bulgarians (First and Second Empires)
entries.region: Balkans: the Danube to the Balkan mountains
entries.settlement: fortified capitals (Pliska, Preslav, Tarnovo); Orthodox monasteries; village communes
entries.beliefs: Tengrism to 864, then Orthodox Christianity; independent Bulgarian church from 870
entries.fell_by: Ottoman conquest 1396 ended the Second Empire; liberated 1878/1908
entries.notes: Gave the Slavs their alphabet; the medieval Bulgarian empire twice rivaled Byzantium.

entries.name: Serbs
entries.region: Western Balkans (Raska, Zeta, Morava valleys)
entries.settlement: monastic charter towns; zadruga (joint-family) villages; Ottoman-border hajduk lands
entries.beliefs: Orthodox Christianity
entries.fell_by: Kosovo 1389 and Ottoman conquest 1459; liberated 1804-1830s
entries.notes: Guardian of Orthodox identity under Ottoman rule; the epic memory of Kosovo shaped the nation.

entries.name: Romanians (Vlachs)
entries.region: Carpathians and Danube delta; Wallachia, Moldavia, Transylvania
entries.settlement: shepherd villages; boyar courts; fortified Saxon towns in Transylvania
trade: salt, livestock and grain to the Danube and Black Sea
entries.beliefs: Orthodox Christianity; in Transylvania mixed with Catholic and Protestant
entries.fell_by: Ottoman vassalage 15th-19th c.; Phanariot rule; unified Romanian state 1859
entries.notes: Romance language and people surrounded by Slavs and Magyars; shepherds moved flocks between mountain summer and lowland winter pastures.

entries.name: Cossacks
entries.region: Ukrainian and south Russian steppes (Zaporozhia, Don, Kuban)
entries.settlement: slobodas (free settlements) and the Sich, a fortified camp-republic; self-governing military democracies
entries.beliefs: Orthodox Christianity; a brotherhood sworn by the cross
entries.fell_by: not conquered: the Sich was destroyed by Catherine II in 1775 and Cossacks were absorbed into the Russian Empire
entries.notes: The word is Turkic: qazaq, a free man or wanderer. Frontier republics of runaway serfs and steppe warriors.

entries.name: Romani (Roma)
entries.region: arrived from northwest India c. 1000-1100; diaspora across the Balkans and Eastern Europe
subsistence: crafts for hire: metalwork, horse trading
entries.settlement: nomadic camps of vardo wagons; settled mahala quarters in towns
monuments: none (no permanent stone architecture; memory carried in song)
entries.beliefs: folk Christianity or Islam layered over older Indian and shamanic strata; ancestor cults
entries.fell_by: never a state; enslaved in Wallachia and Moldavia until 1856; the Porajmos (genocide) 1941-45
entries.notes: Europe's largest stateless people; names are borrowed from host languages, so they vary by country.

entries.name: Scythians
entries.region: Pontic-Caspian steppe, from the Danube to the Don
entries.settlement: nomadic camps and royal barrows; hillfort capitals (Scythian Neapolis); trade at Greek Olbia
monuments: Solokha and Tolstaya Mohyla royal kurgans
trade: grain and hides to the Greek Black Sea colonies
Greek wine, silver and olive oil in
entries.beliefs: sky god (Papaios), hearth goddess, ancestor and horse cults; hemp-smoke rituals
entries.fell_by: Sarmatian incursion from the east; absorbed by c. 200 BCE
entries.notes: Hellenized Iranian nomads of the Black Sea steppe; their gold fills the Hermitage.

entries.name: Sarmatians
entries.region: Pontic-Caspian steppe, north of the Black Sea
subsistence: raiding into the Balkans and Parthia
entries.settlement: nomadic camps; no cities; kurgans for the elite
monuments: kurgans of the Don and Volga steppes
trade: steppe goods to Rome and Parthia
entries.beliefs: Iranian religion; venerated the sword planted in the ground; fire cult
entries.fell_by: Hunnic destruction of the Pontic steppe from 372 CE; remnants absorbed into the Hungarians and Alans
entries.notes: The heavy-cavalry culture Rome called on first; their long sword ancestor fed into medieval European sword design.

entries.name: Alans
entries.region: North Caucasus and Pontic steppe; later Gaul and Iberia
entries.settlement: nomadic camps; fortified Alan strongholds in the Caucasus (Maghas)
monuments: Maghas, the Alan capital of the Caucasus
trade: mercenary contracts with Rome, Byzantium and Armenia
entries.beliefs: Iranian religion with a sword cult; later Orthodox Christianity in the Caucasus
entries.fell_by: Hunnic conquest drove them west in 372 CE; Caucasus remnants survive as the Ossetians
entries.notes: Ossetians are their living descendants; Alanic cavalry echoes in Hungarian and Polish lore.

entries.name: Huns
entries.region: Pontic steppe and Pannonia; empire from the Volga to the Rhine
entries.settlement: a huge mobile ordo (camp) around the khagan's tent; subject villages paid tribute
monuments: none identified; the Pannonian capitals are not securely located
entries.beliefs: steppe shamanism; sky god Tangri; ancestor cult and horse sacrifice
entries.fell_by: Attila's death 453; the revolt at Nedao 454; the empire disintegrated within a generation
entries.notes: Europe's first steppe empire; the name became a byword for terror and horsemanship.

entries.name: Pannonian Avars
entries.region: Pannonia (modern Hungary and western Romania)
entries.settlement: ring-shaped fortified camps (the Hring); the khagan's court; Slav foederati villages
entries.beliefs: steppe shamanism; Tengri
entries.fell_by: Charlemagne's campaigns 791-796 broke the Hring; remnants absorbed by the Magyars and Slavs
entries.notes: Ruled Pannonia for over two centuries; brought stirrups and sabretaches to Europe.

entries.name: Volga Bulgars
entries.region: Middle Volga (modern Tatarstan)
entries.settlement: walled trading towns, Bolghar and Suvar; river ports on the Volga
monuments: Bolghar: the Great Minaret and the Northern Mausoleum
trade: furs, honey, wax and leather to the Islamic world and Kievan Rus'
silver dirhams, cloth and spices in
entries.beliefs: Tengrism, then Islam, adopted 922 (Ibn Fadlan's embassy)
entries.fell_by: destroyed by the Mongols in 1236; survivors became the Kazan Tatars and the Chuvash
entries.notes: The first Muslim state in the Volga basin; their leather was prized from Baghdad to Novgorod.

entries.name: Khazars
entries.region: Lower Volga, North Caucasus and the Pontic steppe
entries.settlement: Itil, the capital in the Volga delta; Samandar; the fortress of Sarkel
trade: the artery between Scandinavia, Kievan Rus', Byzantium and the Caliphate
furs and silks; customs collected at Itil
entries.beliefs: eclectic, then Judaism among the elite c. 740-860; Tengrism, Islam and Christianity among subjects
entries.fell_by: Svyatoslav of Kyiv sacked Itil and Sarkel in 965-969; remnants absorbed by the Volga Bulgars and Kipchaks
entries.notes: The khaganate that taxed the Silk Road; Ibn Fadlan and a Hebrew letter of c. 950 describe its court.

entries.name: Pechenegs
entries.region: Pontic steppe, from the Danube to the Don
entries.settlement: eight tribal confederations arranged in wings; camps along the Dnieper and Danube
monuments: none surviving; kurgan groups in the steppe
trade: slaves sold to Byzantium and Hungary
controlled Rus' trade on the Dnieper
entries.beliefs: steppe shamanism; Tengri
entries.fell_by: crushed by the Cumans at Levounion in 1091 (with Byzantium and Hungary); survivors fled west
entries.notes: For two centuries the terror of the Rus' trade route to Constantinople; Svyatoslav died in their ambush in 972.

entries.name: Cumans (Kipchaks, Polovtsy)
entries.region: Pontic-Caspian steppe (Desht-i Qipchaq)
entries.settlement: no fixed cities; seasonal migration routes; Cuman khan families intermarried with Rus' and Hungarian nobles
monuments: Cuman 'baba' stone statues scattered over the steppe
entries.beliefs: Tengrism; shamanism; ancestral 'baba' stone idols
entries.fell_by: Mongol conquest 1237-1242; refugees fled to Hungary (the Kunsag) and Bulgaria
entries.notes: The steppe confederation the Rus' chronicles called the Polovtsy; Bonyak raided Kyiv's borders for a generation.

entries.name: Golden Horde (Ulus of Jochi)
entries.region: Volga-Ural and Pontic steppes; overlord of the Rus' principalities
subsistence: tribute from Rus' (the vykhod, paid in silver)
entries.settlement: Sarai and Sarai Berke on the Volga; the yam relay-post road network; trading towns
trade: Silk Road and Black Sea trade; the Genoese Crimea colonies as brokers
entries.beliefs: Tengrism to 1313, then Islam (under Özbeg Khan); the Rus' Orthodox Church was exempt from tribute
entries.fell_by: disintegrated into the Kazan, Astrakhan and Crimean khanates; the last khan, Ahmad, was defeated in 1502
entries.notes: A quarter-millennium of Mongol overlordship over Rus'; the yam post and the census shaped Russian administration.

entries.name: Kazan Tatars
entries.region: Middle Volga (Kazan)
entries.settlement: walled Kremlin of Kazan; mosques; dense village networks
monuments: Kazan Kremlin and the Soembike Tower
entries.beliefs: Islam (Sunni)
entries.fell_by: conquered by Ivan IV in 1552; survivors absorbed into the Russian Empire; still a distinct people
entries.notes: Heir to both the Volga Bulgars and the Golden Horde; Kazan fell to Moscow's siege in 1552.

entries.name: Crimean Tatars (Khanate of Crimea)
entries.region: Crimea and the northern Black Sea steppe
subsistence: trade; raiding for captives sold to Ottoman markets
entries.settlement: the palace-city of Bakhchisarai; fortified hamlets; allied with the Ottomans
monuments: Bakhchisarai Palace of the Khans (with the Fountain of Tears)
trade: captives to the Ottoman slave markets
entries.beliefs: Islam (Sunni)
entries.fell_by: annexed by Russia in 1783; mass deportation by Stalin in 1944; returned in the 1990s
entries.notes: The last khanate of the Golden Horde; nearly a third of Crimea's Tatars were deported in 1944 and half died on the way.

entries.name: Lipka Tatars (Lithuanian Tatars)
entries.region: Lithuania, Poland and Belarus (lands of the Grand Duchy)
entries.settlement: small Muslim villages and Tatar quarters in Vilnius, Trakai and Minsk
entries.beliefs: Islam (Sunni), practiced in a Christian state
entries.fell_by: never a state; largely assimilated over the centuries; dispersed again in 1945
entries.notes: Vytautas settled Golden Horde captives in Lithuania; their light cavalry fought at Grunwald in 1410.

entries.name: Nogais
entries.region: Volga-Ural steppes and the North Caucasus (the Nogai Steppe)
entries.settlement: nomadic auls on the Volga and the Yaik (Ural)
entries.beliefs: Islam (Sunni)
entries.fell_by: Muscovite expansion 16th-17th c.; Astrakhan fell 1556; the horde broke into rival Nogai hordes
entries.notes: Descendants of the Golden Horde; Moscow's earliest relations with the steppe ran through them.

entries.name: Bashkirs
entries.region: Southern Urals and the Belaya river forest-steppe
entries.settlement: nomadic auls along river valleys; semi-sedentary from the 18th c.
monuments: none of stone; the Ural-batur epic is their monument
entries.beliefs: Tengrism then Islam (14th c.)
entries.fell_by: never a state; citizenship to Muscovy from 1557; revolts in 1704-1711 and Pugachev's war, 1773-75; autonomous republic since 1919
entries.notes: Wild-honey tree-climbers; the Bashkir horse is one of the hardiest steppe breeds.

entries.name: Kazakhs (Kazakh Khanate)
entries.region: The Kazakh steppe, from the Urals to the Altai
entries.settlement: nomadic auls organized into three zhuzes (hordes): Senior, Middle, Junior
monuments: Mausoleum of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi, Turkestan
trade: caravan traffic on the Silk Road
entries.beliefs: Islam (Sunni), layered over Tengri and shamanism
entries.fell_by: absorbed into the Russian Empire 1731-1868; famine and upheaval under Soviet rule; independent in 1991
entries.notes: Qazaq means free man, the same root as Cossack; the three hordes structured all steppe politics.

entries.name: Kyrgyz
entries.region: Tian Shan and Pamir-Alay; originally the upper Yenisei
entries.settlement: high-altitude seasonal jailoo camps; no capitals, everything moved
monuments: none of stone; the Manas epic (500,000 lines) is the archive
entries.beliefs: Tengri and shamanism, then Islam (Sunni); manaschi (epic singers) as sacred figures
entries.fell_by: never one state; incorporated into the Russian Empire in the 1860s; independent in 1991
entries.notes: The Manas epic is twenty times the Iliad; Kyrgyz berkut eagles still hunt fox on the steppe.

entries.name: Ostrogoths
entries.region: Ukrainian forest-steppe, later Italy
entries.settlement: forest-steppe hillforts (Chernyakhov culture); later the capital at Ravenna
monuments: Theodoric's Mausoleum, Ravenna; Chernyakhov sites on the Dnieper
entries.beliefs: Gothic paganism, then Arian Christianity (Ulfilas translated the Bible c. 360)
entries.fell_by: Hunnic subjection from 375; collapse in Italy after Theodoric's death 526; the Lombards broke the kingdom in 568
entries.notes: The Chernyakhov culture gave them an empire; Ulfilas's Gothic Bible was Europe's first Bible in a vernacular.

entries.name: Cimmerians
entries.region: Pontic steppe, north of the Black Sea
entries.settlement: nomadic camps; no cities
monuments: none identified; Crimean 'Cimmerian' barrows are disputed
crafts: the first animal-art of the steppe
entries.beliefs: steppe shamanism
entries.fell_by: Scythian displacement c. 700 BCE; remnants absorbed into Scythia
entries.notes: The steppe's first named people; the Greeks named the Kerch strait the Kimmerios Bosporos after them.

entries.name: Varangians (Rus')
entries.region: Scandinavian traders on the eastern rivers, from the Baltic to Constantinople
entries.settlement: river ports: Staraya Ladoga, Novgorod, Kyiv; longphorts along the Volkhov and Dnieper
monuments: Staraya Ladoga; the burial mounds at Gnezdovo
trade: amber, furs and slaves to Byzantium and the Islamic world
silk, silver and wine in; the route from the Varangians to the Greeks
entries.beliefs: Norse paganism, then Orthodox Christianity (Vladimir, 988)
entries.fell_by: assimilated into East Slavic culture by the 11th c.; the name Rus' gave Russia its name
entries.notes: Swedes on the rivers; Byzantium hired them as the Varangian Guard, where they wielded battle-axes.

entries.name: Old Prussians
entries.region: Southeast Baltic (modern Kaliningrad, northeast Poland)
entries.settlement: fortified hillforts (pilis); small tribal districts; no state
monuments: the Romuva sanctuary (Romove) described by chroniclers
trade: amber down the Amber Road to the Mediterranean
entries.beliefs: Baltic paganism; Perkunas the thunder-god; sacred oaks
entries.fell_by: Teutonic Order conquest 1230-1283; plague and assimilation; their language extinct by about 1700
entries.notes: The westernmost Balts; their amber traveled from the Baltic to pharaohs' tombs.

entries.name: Estonians
entries.region: Baltic Estonia
entries.settlement: fortified hillforts (linnamagi); village communes; Danish and German conquest 1219-1227
trade: herring and rye through the Baltic; the Hanseatic port of Tallinn
entries.beliefs: Finnic shamanism to the 1220s, then Catholicism
entries.fell_by: Danish and German conquest 1219-1227; 700 years of Danish, Swedish and Russian rule; independent in 1918
entries.notes: A Finnic people, cousins of the Finns; the St George's Night rising of 1343 was crushed.

entries.name: Mari and Mordvins
entries.region: The Volga-Oka forest belt (Mari El, Mordovia)
entries.settlement: kin-based forest-edge villages; pre-conquest hillforts
entries.beliefs: Finno-Permic shamanism; the Mari still sacrifice in sacred groves to Osh Kugu Jumo, the White Great God
entries.fell_by: Volga Bulgar and then Mongol domination; Russian conquest 13th-16th c.; autonomous republics today
entries.notes: Europe's last pagans: Mari groves still host sacrifices; Mordvins are the easternmost Finno-Ugric farmlanders.

entries.name: Khanty and Mansi
entries.region: Western Siberia, the Ob river basin (taiga and forest-tundra)
entries.settlement: seasonal camps; summer fishing villages; winter smokehouse camps
monuments: none; Ob-Ugric cult sites and sacred islets on the Ob
trade: sable and other furs to Novgorod and Muscovy
entries.beliefs: Ob-Ugric shamanism; the bear cult; the god Torum
entries.fell_by: never a state; Russian fur tribute (yasak) from the 16th c.; autonomous district since 1930
entries.notes: Ob-Ugric peoples; the Mansi were known to Russians as the Voguls, source of the Vogulka in folk tales.

entries.name: Chuvash
entries.region: Volga-Sura forest-steppe (Chuvashia)
entries.settlement: wooden-house villages with communal assemblies; heirs to Volga Bulgar towns
monuments: their architecture is wood; they inherit the Bulgar ruins at Bolghar
trade: furs and honey; the Volga Bulgar trade successor
entries.beliefs: a surviving Turkic paganism (Old Chuvash faith), later Orthodox Christianity
entries.fell_by: absorbed into the Golden Horde and Kazan spheres; mass Orthodox conversion in the 18th c.; autonomous since 1920
entries.notes: The only Turkic people speaking an r-language (the Bulgar branch); the closest living relative of the Volga Bulgars.

entries.name: Sorbs (Wends)
entries.region: Lusatia, eastern Germany and western Poland
entries.settlement: village communes absorbed into medieval German lordships
monuments: none; the Krabat folk tales are Sorbian
entries.beliefs: Slavic paganism to about 1000, then Catholicism; Vogelhochzeit (bird wedding) customs survive
entries.fell_by: German eastward expansion 12th-13th c.; assimilation; a Sorbian minority of about 60,000 survives in Germany
entries.notes: The last Slavs in Germany; Upper and Lower Sorbian are written languages; Wend was the German exonym.

entries.name: Crimean Goths (Gothia)
entries.region: The southwestern Crimea, the Gothic mountain country
entries.settlement: hillforts and mountain retreats, chiefly Doros (later Mangup)
entries.beliefs: Gothic paganism, then Arianism, then Orthodox Christianity
entries.fell_by: Turkic pressure 8th-15th c.; deportation and absorption; the last speakers were recorded in the 16th c.
entries.notes: A Germanic language still spoken in Crimea in 1562; Busbecq's wordlist (ada for brother) is its last record.
